# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) has become a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention in patients at risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs), however, carry well-recognized risks related to the intravascular leads, including vascular injury, pneumothorax, lead fracture, and most importantly, systemic infection and the morbidity of lead extraction [2,3]. The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these complications by eliminating the need for intravascular or intracardiac hardware [4]. Since its introduction and subsequent CE marking and FDA approval, the S-ICD has emerged as an established alternative for selected patients requiring defibrillation without pacing [5].

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD comprises a pulse generator implanted in a lateral subcutaneous or intermuscular pocket and a single parasternal lead positioned subcutaneously [4]. The system delivers an 80-J shock and provides post-shock transthoracic pacing but cannot offer long-term bradycardia pacing, anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization [6]. The original demonstration of the concept showed that subcutaneous shocks could reliably terminate ventricular fibrillation in humans [4]. This design is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with limited venous access, prior device infections, or those at high lifetime risk of lead complications [7].

## Clinical Evidence

Early experience from the EFFORTLESS registry and the IDE study demonstrated favorable conversion efficacy and acceptable complication rates [5,8]. Pooled analyses confirmed high rates of successful conversion of induced ventricular arrhythmias and effective treatment of spontaneous episodes [9]. The pivotal randomized comparison came from the PRAETORIAN trial, which compared the S-ICD with the TV-ICD in patients with an indication for defibrillation but no pacing requirement [10]. The S-ICD was noninvasive to the heart and proved noninferior with respect to the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [10]. Long-term follow-up reinforced the durability of these findings [11].

The UNTOUCHED study specifically evaluated inappropriate shock rates in a primary-prevention population with low ejection fraction using contemporary programming, demonstrating markedly reduced inappropriate shock rates compared with earlier reports [12]. These data underscored the importance of dual-zone programming and modern sensing algorithms in minimizing inappropriate therapy [13].

## Patient Selection and Screening

Appropriate patient selection is critical to S-ICD success [14]. Because sensing is performed via surface-like electrograms, preimplant electrocardiographic screening is mandatory to ensure adequate vector signals and avoid T-wave oversensing [15]. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, channelopathies, and other inherited arrhythmia syndromes are often ideal candidates given their younger age and lack of pacing need [16,17]. Conversely, patients requiring bradycardia pacing, ATP for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, or resynchronization are generally unsuitable [6]. Exercise screening may improve identification of patients at risk of inappropriate sensing [18].

## Complications and Limitations

Although the S-ICD avoids intravascular complications, it is not without drawbacks. Inappropriate shocks, historically driven by T-wave oversensing and supraventricular arrhythmias, remain a concern, though refined SMART Pass filtering has reduced their incidence [13,19]. Device-related infections still occur but rarely involve the bloodstream, simplifying management compared with transvenous systems [20]. The generator is larger and the implant pocket can cause discomfort or erosion [21]. The inability to deliver ATP means some patients experience shocks for arrhythmias that might otherwise be painlessly terminated [22].

## Implantation Technique and Innovations

The intermuscular two-incision technique has largely replaced the original three-incision approach, improving cosmesis and reducing complications [23]. Defibrillation testing at implant, once routine, is now individualized given PRAETORIAN-based risk scoring of implant position via chest radiography [24]. The PRAETORIAN score allows assessment of adequate device positioning without routine defibrillation testing [24].

## Future Directions

A major limitation—the absence of pacing—is being addressed by the integration of the S-ICD with leadless pacemakers to provide communicating ATP and bradycardia support [25]. The modular cardiac rhythm management system combining a leadless pacemaker with the S-ICD has shown feasibility in early trials [26]. Continued miniaturization, improved battery longevity, and enhanced discrimination algorithms are anticipated [27]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest the S-ICD is economically reasonable in appropriately selected patients, particularly those at high infection risk [28]. Guidelines now incorporate the S-ICD as a recommended option for patients without pacing indications [29]. Ongoing real-world registries continue to refine our understanding of long-term outcomes across diverse populations [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents a significant advance in SCD prevention, offering effective defibrillation while avoiding the complications of transvenous leads. Robust randomized and registry data support its noninferiority for appropriately selected patients. As leadless pacing integration matures, the S-ICD's principal limitation may soon be overcome, broadening its applicability in clinical practice.
